data.content_ref: inline:The claim asserts that Popper's preference for better-corroborated theories is 'defensible on his own terms as a non-inductive, methodological rule for maximizing verisimilitude.' Yet the target's own first countercondition acknowledges that if the formal definition of verisimilitude is logically incoherent for comparing false theories — as Tichý and Miller independently demonstrated — then 'the claim that corroboration tracks truth-likeness collapses.' This is not merely an external objection; it strikes the very foundation the claim uses to justify the defense. Popper himself conceded after the Tichý/Miller results that his formal definition of verisimilitude was flawed. If the concept of verisimilitude cannot coherently compare false theories, then the claim's central assertion that corroboration 'maximizes verisimilitude' is vacuous: the methodological rule has no determinate target to maximize. The claim thus asserts the defense is 'defensible on his own terms' while simultaneously embedding a countercondition that, if satisfied, makes the defense fail on exactly those terms. The claim never resolves this tension — it simply lists the fatal condition alongside the assertion it would defeat. An argument that declares a position defensible while acknowledging an unresolved condition under which its core justificatory concept is incoherent has not actually mounted a defense; it has merely deferred the question.
